original_question: Let f (x) ∈ Q(x) be a rational function of degree d ≥ 2, and for each prime p, let f˜p ∈ Fp (x) denote its reduction modulo p; see Section 12. (a) Is it true that the set (19.3) p : f˜p (x) is stable over Fp is a finite set? (b) Is it true that the set (19.4) p : f˜p (x) is eventually stable over Fp is a finite set? As a specific example, Jones [122, Conjecture 6.3] has conjectured that x2 + 1 is stable over Fp if and only if p = 3, i.e., for f (x) = x2 + 1, the set (19.3) is {3}. Ferraguti [76] has shown that under some Galois-theoretic assumptions, the set of stable primes (19.3) has density zero.
target_in_paper: Section 19, Question 19.12, together with Definitions 19.1 and 19.2 and the finite-field base-point-0 convention in the paragraph immediately preceding Question 19.11; the reduction notation comes from Section 12, Definition 12.2 and Remark 12.3.
correct_elements: The draft correctly targets the exact open problem stated in the paper: Question 19.12 in Section 19. It has the right ambient object f in Q(x), the correct degree condition d >= 2, the reduction mod p to a map over F_p, and the two precise finiteness questions about the sets of stable and eventually stable primes. It also accurately preserves the paper's nearby motivating example for f(x)=x^2+1 and the Ferraguti density-zero remark.
missing_details: In the finite-field discussion, the paper is implicitly talking about the pair (tilde f_p, 0) on P^1; the base point 0 is suppressed because the paragraph before Question 19.11 notes that an affine change of coordinates reduces the general base point to 0.
The notion of 'stable over F_p' needs to be made explicit: if tilde f_p^n(x) = F_{n,p}(x)/G_{n,p}(x) in lowest terms, then stability means that F_{n,p}(x) is irreducible in F_p[x] for every n >= 1.
The notion of 'eventually stable over F_p' also needs to be defined: there exists m >= 0 such that for every beta in tilde f_p^{-m}(0), the pair (tilde f_p, beta) is stable over F_p(beta).
The paper explicitly records an equivalent bounded-factor formulation of eventual stability, and that equivalence is useful for making part (b) stand alone.
Reduction modulo p should be specified in the Section 12 sense, namely by choosing a normalized integral model of f on P^1 and reducing coefficients modulo p.
The draft leaves implicit how to treat primes where reduction lowers the degree of f, a possibility explicitly noted in Section 12.
refined_question: Let f(x) be a rational function in Q(x) of degree d >= 2, represented on P^1 by a normalized integral model, and for each prime p let tilde f_p in F_p(x) be its reduction modulo p as in Section 12. For every prime p with deg(tilde f_p) >= 2, write tilde f_p^n(x) = F_{n,p}(x)/G_{n,p}(x) in lowest terms. Using the paper's finite-field convention that stability is considered at base point 0, say that (tilde f_p, 0) is stable over F_p if F_{n,p}(x) is irreducible in F_p[x] for every n >= 1, and say that (tilde f_p, 0) is eventually stable over F_p if there exists m >= 0 such that for every beta in tilde f_p^{-m}(0), the pair (tilde f_p, beta) is stable over F_p(beta). Is the set of primes p for which (tilde f_p, 0) is stable over F_p finite? Is the set of primes p for which (tilde f_p, 0) is eventually stable over F_p finite?
equivalent_formulation: For part (b), the paper states the equivalent reformulation that (tilde f_p, 0) is eventually stable over F_p if and only if there exists a constant C_p such that, for every n >= 1, the numerator F_{n,p}(x) of tilde f_p^n(x) has at most C_p irreducible factors in F_p[x], counted with multiplicity. In this language, part (a) is the special case where every F_{n,p}(x) is irreducible.
justification: The draft is already very close to the official formulation: it is essentially Question 19.12 verbatim. What prevents it from being fully stand-alone is that the paper's surrounding text supplies the hidden conventions and definitions: Section 12 explains what 'reduction modulo p' means, Definitions 19.1 and 19.2 define stability and eventual stability, and the paragraph before Question 19.11 explains that over finite fields one may normalize to base point 0 by affine conjugacy. The refined version inserts exactly those paper-local ingredients and does not broaden the question beyond the scope of Question 19.12.
